lesson.title: How a Computer Talks to the World
lesson.summary: Input and output devices are the physical bridge between people and a computer's CPU and memory, turning human actions into signals the machine can process and turning results back into something a person can see, hear, or feel.
lesson.body:
A computer's CPU and memory can only work with electrical signals arranged into binary patterns. People, on the other hand, communicate by pressing keys, moving a mouse, speaking, and touching screens. Input and output devices exist to translate between these two worlds. An input device converts a physical action into a digital signal the computer can process, and an output device converts a digital signal back into something a human can perceive.

Common input devices include the keyboard, mouse, microphone, camera, and touchscreen. Common output devices include the monitor, speakers, and printer. Some devices do both jobs at once. A touchscreen accepts taps and swipes as input while also displaying pixels as output. A network interface card sends data out to other computers and receives data coming in, so it counts as both input and output depending on the direction data is moving.

It helps to trace one keystroke all the way through the system, because the same basic pipeline applies to almost every input and output device. Suppose you press the letter A on a keyboard. The keyboard has its own small controller chip that detects which physical switch closed and generates a code identifying that key, called a scancode. The keyboard sends this scancode over a cable or wireless link to the computer, where it triggers an interrupt, a signal that tells the CPU to pause what it is doing and handle new input. The operating system's keyboard driver reads the scancode and translates it into the character A, then stores that character in memory as part of whatever program is currently accepting text. If that program needs to display the letter, it asks the graphics hardware to update the pixels on the monitor at the right location, and the monitor lights up the correct arrangement of pixels so your eyes can see the letter A appear. All of this happens in a small fraction of a second.

This chain only works because of the hardware you already know about from CPU and memory. The CPU is the component that actually decides what to do with incoming data, and memory is where that data is temporarily held so the CPU can read and write it quickly. Input and output devices are the entry and exit points to that CPU and memory system. Without them, a computer would have no way to receive instructions from a person or to show that person any result, no matter how fast its processor was.

It is also worth noticing that input and output devices connect to the rest of the computer through standardized ports and buses, such as USB, HDMI, or a wireless protocol like Bluetooth. Standardization matters because it means a keyboard made by one company and a computer made by another can still communicate, as long as both follow the same protocol for encoding and transmitting signals. This same idea of standardized interfaces shows up again later when you learn about operating systems, since one of the operating system's jobs is to provide a consistent way for software to talk to many different brands and models of input and output hardware without each program needing to know the electrical details of every device.
